# Summary of Information on Lynn Conway
Lynn Conway, born in 1938 in Mount Vernon, New York, is a pioneering computer scientist and transgender rights activist. After facing gender dysphoria early in life and an initial attempted transition at MIT that was withdrawn, she resumed her transition in 1967 under the care of Harry Benjamin. Conway was fired from IBM in 1968 after revealing her intention to transition, and IBM later issued a public apology and awarded her a Lifetime Achievement Award in 2020. Post-transition, she rebuilt her career starting as a contract programmer and digital system designer, eventually joining Xerox PARC in 1973. There, she led significant advancements in VLSI (very-large-scale integration) design, collaborating with Carver Mead and Ivan Sutherland. Their work culminated in the groundbreaking textbook *Introduction to VLSI Systems* (1980), which became a standard in chip design education.
Conway also founded the multiproject wafers (MPW) technology and helped establish MOSIS, an internet-based infrastructure for rapid prototyping and fabrication of chip designs, institutionalized in 1981. She taught at MIT in 1978, validating and propagating the Mead-Conway design methodology globally. Her contributions sparked a revolution in semiconductor technology and the electronic design automation industry, influencing numerous startups in subsequent decades. As an activist, Conway publicly shared her gender transition story in 1999 and engaged extensively in transgender rights advocacy, providing resources, critique of prevailing typologies, and campaigning for inclusion in professional ethics codes. Recognized as a "Stonewall 40 trans hero" in 2009 and named in Time Magazine's list of influential transgender individuals, she has been honored by various academic and professional organizations. Conway passed away in 2024 at the age of 86.
